extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists, and professionals (legal and mental-health) researching false allegations of child sexual abuse
extracted.subtask_description: A general encyclopedic overview of false allegations of child sexual abuse covering definitions, types, causes, prevalence estimates, legal effects (UK), impacts on victims and the accused, support groups, and media portrayals. Intended as an informational summary rather than procedural guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of false allegation of child sexual abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: A false allegation of child sexual abuse is "an accusation against one or more individuals claiming that they committed child sexual abuse when no abuse has been committed by the accused." Such accusations can be brought by the alleged victim or by another person on the alleged victim's behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes studies from the 1990s suggesting an overall rate of false accusations of approximately 10%, and emphasizes that denials by the accused should not be interpreted as evidence of guilt. It frames false allegations as a distinct phenomenon from unsubstantiated or unfounded reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completely false allegation (events did not occur)
rubrics_metrics.description: An allegation that is completely false in that the events that were alleged did not occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given include motivations such as retaliation (e.g., against a teacher or employer), extortion, or blackmail. This category is presented as one of three primary types of allegations determined to be false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetrator substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: An allegation that describes events that did occur, but were perpetrated by an individual who is not accused; when a child makes this type of allegation it is termed 'perpetrator substitution.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This category emphasizes that the factual events may be real but the accused person is innocent because someone else committed the acts described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partially true / partially false allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations that are partially true and partially false, mixing descriptions of events that actually happened with other events that did not occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizes that not all false allegations are entirely fabricated; some contain elements of truth combined with incorrect or invented elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes: intentional lying, confabulation, and suggestive interviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: False allegations can result from intentional lying by the accuser or unintentionally via confabulation (from mental illness) or from suggestive questioning, coaching of the child, or faulty interviewing techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites Poole and Lindsay (1997) proposing separate labels: 'false allegations' when the accuser is aware they are lying, and 'false suspicions' for a wider range including suggestive-questioning cases. It highlights how interviewing practices and coaching can create false reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of officials and confirmation bias in prompting/perpetuating false accusations
rubrics_metrics.description: Law enforcement, child protection, or prosecution officials can prompt, aggravate or perpetuate false accusations when they become convinced of the accused's guilt and disregard disconfirming evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes how cognitive dissonance can lead officials to ignore, discount, or destroy disconfirming evidence, making it difficult to revisit verdicts and potentially continuing through appeals or retrials. It references 'trawling' practices and incentives (e.g., compensation) that can increase false allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitated communication as a source of false accusations
rubrics_metrics.description: Facilitated communication (FC) is a scientifically discredited technique used to aid non-verbal people (e.g., with autism) in typing or communicating; research shows the facilitator is the sole source of messages obtained by FC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes the ideomotor effect as the mechanism and documents numerous accusations of sexual abuse made through FC (about sixty known cases as of 1995), illustrating how pseudoscientific techniques can generate false allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence and methodological variability in false allegation rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies between 1987 and 1995 reported false allegation rates from 6% to 35% of reported child sexual abuse cases; a 1992 meta-analysis suggested between 2% and 10% of all allegations. Rates vary widely depending on the criteria used (intentional lying vs. inclusion of unintentional false allegations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains that reporting rates may be substantially below actual rates of abuse (underreporting) which complicates estimation, and that false reports are more common in custody disputes. It attributes variability to differing study definitions and methods, and warns against simplistic interpretations of prevalence figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: False retractions: causes and protective factors
rubrics_metrics.description: False retractions (children retracting true allegations) may occur due to shame, fear of foster care, desire to protect a perpetrator (often a family member), fear of destroying the family, coaching by adults to withdraw accusations, and similar pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states false retractions are less common when the child receives timely and appropriate support following the allegation, indicating support as a mitigating factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of changes to legal tests (UK) — similar fact evidence and 'corroboration by volume'
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1991 House of Lords judgment (D.P.P. v P) lowered the barrier to admission of similar fact evidence of disposition in sexual-abuse cases, effectively allowing 'corroboration by volume' rather than requiring 'striking similarities' linking allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page links this legal change and police 'trawling' practices to increased opportunities and incentives for false allegations. It notes parliamentary and committee debates and recommendations (e.g., Home Affairs Select Committee) to restore a higher threshold for similar fact evidence in historical child-abuse cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on the child and the accused
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations (including false ones) can be inherently traumatic to the child; people falsely charged often face social stigma, job loss, damaged relationships, harassment, property vandalism or confiscation, and other severe consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes the lasting and devastating effects on families and children, including increased risk of child alienation from a parent, and notes public tendency to assume guilt in highly publicized cases. It reiterates that denial should not be read as evidence of guilt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support groups and advocacy for the falsely accused
rubrics_metrics.description: There are support and lobby groups established to redress perceived injustices suffered by those who claim to have been wrongly convicted or accused of abuse; the article lists several UK groups (e.g., FACT, FASO, PAFAA, SAFARI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as part of the social response landscape; groups provide support, lobbying, and public advocacy for those affected by false allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media and cultural portrayals of false allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: The article lists films and documentaries that depict false accusations (e.g., Take Me to the River, The Hunt / Jagten, Capturing the Friedmans, A Map of the World, Serious Charge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples illustrate how false-allegation cases enter public consciousness and can shape perceptions, contributing to public debates about child-abuse investigations and miscarriages of justice.
